extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalists, researchers, and fact‑checkers investigating disinformation and influence operations
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and cataloging signals that a website or network is part of a coordinated disinformation / influence operation (e.g., ghost outlets, content farms, PR‑linked networks). Focuses on observable site characteristics, sourcing/attribution, takedown history, and thematic behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinated inauthentic behavior takedowns
rubrics_metrics.description: Related social media accounts and pages were taken down by Facebook/Twitter in 2020–2021 for coordinated inauthentic behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page repeatedly uses platform takedowns for "coordinated inauthentic behavior" (examples: networks tied to Tunisia/Operation Carthage, Begemot, Luhansk networks) as evidence that a set of sites/accounts formed an influence operation. Use takedown actions and platform attributions as strong signals of coordinated inauthenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Links to public relations or digital marketing firms
rubrics_metrics.description: Operations were traced to public relations firms (e.g., UReputation) or digital marketing firms (DotDev, Smatt, Rep Global) that operated or supported the sites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attribution to named firms (UReputation, DotDev, Smatt, aRep Global, Newave, etc.) is presented as evidence of professional/for‑hire influence campaigns across countries. Notes include geographic spread of firms and cross‑border client work; use corporate links and contractor footprints as indicators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blank or missing 'About' page
rubrics_metrics.description: Some sites have a blank 'About Page' (e.g., Actu France listed as having blank 'About Page').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An empty or intentionally vague About page is flagged repeatedly as a red flag; record absence of credible organizational information as an indicator of inauthentic outlets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalists with no identifiable digital footprint or suspended accounts
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists listed on many sites have accounts that are suspended by Twitter and otherwise have no identifiable digital footprint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeated notes that staffers cannot be independently verified (no social profiles, no prior bylines) are used to question site legitimacy. Suspended social accounts for listed journalists amplify suspicion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copying or recycling content from other news sites
rubrics_metrics.description: Sites copy content from other news websites or recycle articles (examples: copying from Euronews, NewsFront, The Epoch Times).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Content scraping/reposting and heavy reuse of other outlets' material is treated as a sign of content‑farm / junk news behavior rather than original journalism. Note provenance and duplication patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presented as fact‑checking but connected to the network
rubrics_metrics.description: Some domains (e.g., 'Fake News Checking') presented themselves as a fact‑checking outlet while being connected to the identified network (UReputation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Services masquerading as verification or fact‑checking while tied to the network are flagged as deceptive practices; verify independence of fact‑checkers and trace funding/ownership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funding or editorial support by named political actors
rubrics_metrics.description: Sites are described as funded by, supportive of, or linked to named political figures or parties (e.g., funded by Lotfi Bel Hadj; supportive of Faure Gnassingbé; supportive of CCM).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit funding/support links and overt partisan alignment are used to identify politically motivated networks. Track declared/undisclosed funding sources and consistent partisan editorial patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promotion of propaganda tropes and misinformation themes
rubrics_metrics.description: Sites promoted specific false claims or propaganda tropes (examples in text: claims accusing Ukraine of environmental pollution as a 'trope of Russian propaganda', false COVID origin claims, vaccine and COVID‑19 misinformation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recurring thematic tropes (e.g., environmental disaster framing, anti‑vaccine narratives, state‑aligned messaging) indicate coordinated narrative strategies; catalog repeated false narratives and their spread across domains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shared website design or template across multiple domains
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple sites have similar website design indicating a shared operation or template (examples: Revue de l'Afrique, Afrika News, Maghreb Info share similar design).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visual/technical parallels (same templates, styling, CMS footprints) across domains are used as signals of a common operator. Combine with WHOIS, hosting, and infrastructure overlaps for attribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of false copyright/backdating to trigger takedowns
rubrics_metrics.description: Operators added critical Twitter content to blog sites and back‑dated it, then reported the original content to Twitter under the Digital Millennium Copyright Act to remove it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text describes deliberate abuse of DMCA takedown processes and backdating as a tactic to silence critics. Detecting backdated reposts plus DMCA complaints suggests coordinated suppression tactics rather than ordinary copyright disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content‑farm characteristics (low‑effort, high‑volume output)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some networks are characterized as content farms that publish high volumes of recycled or pro‑party content (example: Qiqi News Network described as a content farm).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for high volume, low originality, repetitive headlines, and distribution strategies (e.g., spread over messaging apps like Line) as hallmarks of content‑farm behavior favoring a political viewpoint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alleged links to state actors or government‑aligned groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Several stories/sites are alleged by researchers or governments to be linked directly to state actors or government‑aligned parties (examples: alleged links to the government of the People's Republic of China, Chinese Unification Promotion Party member membership, PRC‑aligned narratives).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims of state linkage (from multiple independent researchers/platform attributions) are used to elevate the severity of influence operations; treat consistent cross‑reporting by reputable analysts as stronger evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification or accusations by research organizations and media
rubrics_metrics.description: Sites/networks are identified or accused by organizations such as Graphika, Stanford Internet Observatory, Digital Forensics Research Lab, Oxford Internet Institute, Global Disinformation Index, Mandiant, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Third‑party identification by established research labs, investigative NGOs, and major media outlets is treated as corroborating evidence. Cite these reports when assessing a network's nature and reach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information laundering and exploitation of legitimate services (newswire, hyperlinks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Campaigns exploited newswire services and hyperlinks to legitimate outlets to amplify content and engage in information laundering (example: Mandiant note about exploiting U.S. news outlets via newswire services).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of legitimate infrastructure (newswires, syndicated feeds, hyperlinking to credible outlets) to hide origin or amplify narratives is a documented tactic; detect whether placement on legitimate channels is organic or engineered.
